newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh strives to revive investors' morale.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh strives to revive investors' morale.

text.p: Bangladesh has ordered a probe into what caused a recent plunge in share prices and will revamp the Securities and Exchange Commission, officials and brokers said on Monday.
Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria called a meeting of stock brokers on Sunday and said an inquiry would take place into reasons behind the bearishness of the stock market.
Kibria said the exchange commission, the market watchdog, would be "restructured in a couple of days" to enable it to act with more efficiency and transparency. He gave no details.
The government would do anything necessary to revive the morale of small investors, Kibria added.
Finance Ministry officials said a committee had been formed to review the market situation and suggest remedial measures to boost market sentiment.
Euphoric trading by thousands of retail investors began around mid-1996 and stemmed from relative political stability and fresh incentives to both foreign and local investors, brokers said.

The Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) benchmark index shot to 3,648.74 points by November 5 in frenzied trading over a three-month period but had dropped to 2,261.47 by Sunday. The index was at 1,145.54 on August 1.
"The bubble has burst," one market analyst said on Monday.
Syed Tareque M. Ali, a stock broker and analyst, blamed government intervention for the recent market doldrums.
"Government intervention is to blame for the unrealistic rise of the market and the recent bearishness," he said.

In October, the exchange commission, alarmed by rising share prices, published a list of "investment-risky" companies and set a price fluctuation limit of 10 percent on shares from the previous day's level.
But a growing number of traders in the kerb market -- which refers to trading that takes place outside official bourse hours -- continued to push share prices up.

Seeing the rise, the stock market watchdog squeezed the price fluctuation limit to five percent in November and the central bank ordered commercial banks to stop offering credit to investors against share certificates, provoking a market slide.
Finance Ministry officials said Kibria has asked the committee to review the market to make recommendations on the effectiveness of the price fluctuation limit, which investors want abolished.
Brokers said traders in the kerb market, who once choked the main street in the Motijheel commercial district, were fewer but remained agitated over heavy losses.
Broker Ali said the market should be free of intervention.

Kibria, in a recent interview with Reuters, said: "No one should expect that the price of the shares will double every week and that there will be windfall. I think this kind of expectation is artificial and unrealistic and has misled many people."
